title: Debug with a Failing Test
subtitle: GitHub Copilot in VS Code · Intermediate

sources.label: Test-driven development with AI in VS Code

scenes.title: State the symptom precisely
scenes.body: Reduce the issue to one input and two observable answers.
scenes.narration: Our synthetic order service accepts an order of zero units. Start by reading the issue and identifying the behavior you can check. If we call the validator with zero, the current answer is true. The expected answer is false. One and five should still pass, and negative one should still fail. Write the expected answer down before opening an agent session.
scenes.code:
is_valid_quantity(0)
Expected: False
Observed: True
scenes.result: Boundary case identified: zero units.

scenes.title: Check the starting suite
scenes.body: Run the existing tests on the starting revision.
scenes.narration: Use the approved runner to execute the existing unit tests. All three pass. Look at the names and compare them with the issue. The tests cover one, five, and negative one. Zero is missing, so a green run provides limited evidence here. Save the test command and starting revision in your notes. You will repeat that command after each change.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_accepts_one ... ok
test_accepts_five ... ok
test_rejects_negative_one ... ok
Ran 3 tests. OK

scenes.title: Turn a guess into a hypothesis
scenes.body: Ask for a prediction tied to a specific line.
scenes.narration: Use Plan with the issue, the validator, and its existing tests in context. Ask Copilot to find the return condition and predict what will happen when zero reaches it. Read that line yourself. The greater-than-or-equal comparison is true at zero. That gives us a prediction we can test. A regression test expecting false for zero should fail on this revision.
scenes.code: return quantity >= 0
scenes.result:
Hypothesis: the equality admits zero.
Prediction: an assertFalse for zero will fail.

scenes.title: Add one test before fixing the code
scenes.body: Inspect the test diff and preserve the original validator.
scenes.narration: Ask Agent to add only the regression test, inside the existing test class. Inspect the diff before running it. The new assertion calls the same public function as the surrounding tests and expects false. Confirm that the validator file has no edit. Then use the approved runner to execute the suite. Keeping the original code for this run lets you check whether the test exposes the reported defect.
scenes.code:
def test_rejects_zero(self):
    self.assertFalse(is_valid_quantity(0))
scenes.result: Changed file: tests/test_order_quantity.py

scenes.title: Read why the test failed
scenes.body: Confirm that the expected assertion failed for zero.
scenes.narration: The new test runs, and the output says true is not false. That matches the predicted behavior on the original code. A failure due to an import error or an empty test run would tell us something different. Check the test name, the assertion, and the total of four tests. Capture this result in your notes so the next run can be compared with it.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false
Ran 4 tests. FAILED (failures=1)

scenes.title: Change the comparison and rerun
scenes.body: The regression and the existing cases should all pass.
scenes.narration: Now apply the smallest change that addresses the hypothesis. Replace greater than or equal to zero with greater than zero and preserve the function signature. Keep the new assertion as written. Rerun the same suite. The output shows the zero test passing with the three earlier tests. Check the diff so your explanation accounts for both changed files and nothing outside the issue.
scenes.code:
-    return quantity >= 0
+    return quantity > 0
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... ok
Ran 4 tests. OK

scenes.title: Leave evidence a teammate can replay
scenes.body: Explain the cause and point to both test runs.
scenes.narration: Write a short handover. Name the input that reproduced the bug, the comparison that caused it, and the command you ran before and after the fix. A teammate should be able to repeat the two runs and get the same result on each revision. As a final check, explain in your own words why one still passes and negative one still fails.
scenes.code:
Input: 0
Cause: equality in the boundary check
Before: one assertion fails
After: four tests pass
scenes.result: A testable explanation of the change.

title: Review a Pull Request with GitHub CLI
subtitle: Human peer review · Intermediate

scenes.title: Start in the reviewer’s account
scenes.body: Confirm the account and the training repository before review.
scenes.narration: In the pilot, the author opened a pull request. Here, you are the teammate reviewing it. Open the approved terminal with your own authorized account and confirm that the GitHub command line is pointed at the training repository. This example uses pull request forty-two. We will inspect the description, the actual patch, and the required checks before you record your own decision.
scenes.code:
gh auth status
gh repo view --json nameWithOwner
scenes.result: Training context confirmed: orders-lab.

scenes.title: Read the intent and the scope
scenes.body: Find the linked issue, the change summary and test evidence.
scenes.narration: Run g h p r view for pull request forty-two. Read what the author says they changed and which issue it closes. Here the business rule is that quantities must be positive, and the public function keeps the same signature. Note the claimed test result. When you read the next command's output, use the issue and its acceptance criteria as the reference.
scenes.code: gh pr view 42
scenes.result:
Reject zero order quantities
Closes #17
Validation: four unit tests passed.

scenes.title: Read the changed lines yourself
scenes.body: Match the implementation and test to the stated behavior.
scenes.narration: Run g h p r diff. The patch should show one changed comparison in the validator and one regression test. Read whether the assertion would have failed before the fix, and check that it exercises the public function. If you see unrelated edits, follow up on why they are present. The author's summary helps you navigate, while the diff is your evidence for what changed.
scenes.code: gh pr diff 42
scenes.result:
-    return quantity >= 0
+    return quantity > 0
+    self.assertFalse(is_valid_quantity(0))

scenes.title: Confirm the configured checks
scenes.body: Review the state of the checks for the current revision.
scenes.narration: Use g h p r checks with the required flag to focus on the checks configured as required for this pull request. Open the relevant run when you need to know what actually executed. If the check is pending, wait for the result. A failing check or missing expected evidence needs investigation. If the author pushes new commits, refresh the diff and checks before deciding.
scenes.code:
gh pr checks 42 --required
gh pr view 42 --json headRefOid
scenes.result:
Unit tests    pass
Head revision recorded for this review.

scenes.title: Request a specific correction
scenes.body: Use this branch of the exercise if the evidence is incomplete.
scenes.narration: Try the alternate scenario. The check is green, but the contributed test never calls the validator with zero. In this case you can request changes and explain the missing assertion. A precise review tells the author what observable behavior to verify. This is one possible decision for the reviewer. Use it when the change needs work, and wait for the next revision before reassessing.
scenes.code:
gh pr review 42 --request-changes \
  --body 'Add a test that calls the validator with zero.'
scenes.result: Record a request with an actionable reason.

scenes.title: Approve when the evidence supports it
scenes.body: The authorized peer submits the review under their own identity.
scenes.narration: Return to the example where the diff matches the issue and the tests cover all four inputs. If that evidence supports your approval, submit it with g h p r review and a concise reason. The human reviewer takes this action. After submitting, confirm that the review was recorded for the pull request. Your approval indicates what you verified at this revision.
scenes.code:
gh pr review 42 --approve \
  --body 'Verified the zero regression and required checks.'
gh pr view 42 --json reviews
scenes.result: Review recorded for the peer account.

scenes.title: Explain the evidence behind your decision
scenes.body: Give a teammate enough detail to verify the review.
scenes.narration: Pair with a teammate and alternate author and reviewer roles on the training repository. The reviewer should be able to state the issue, identify the changed behavior, point to the relevant check, and explain the decision in one sentence. Change only the evidence in a second round and decide again. This gives you practice recognizing when the same looking pull request should receive a different review.
scenes.code: Intent → Diff → Required checks → Decision
scenes.result: A human review with a verifiable reason.

title: Reusable Prompts and Repository Instructions
subtitle: GitHub Copilot in VS Code · Intermediate

scenes.title: Identify what changes from one task to the next
scenes.body: Keep task inputs and durable project conventions easy to find.
scenes.narration: You have planned several small fixes, and the same guidance shows up in your messages. Take one example and mark two kinds of information. The issue number and target behavior belong to the current task. Where tests live and how to run them are conventions for the repository. Keeping them in the right place lets a teammate reuse the guidance without copying an old issue or its assumptions.
scenes.code:
Current task: issue #17 and expected behavior
Repository: tests live in tests/
Repository: use the existing unittest suite
scenes.result: Task inputs and durable conventions identified.

scenes.title: Capture a prompt your team can reuse
scenes.body: Keep a named template and fill in its variable inputs.
scenes.narration: Save this reusable prompt as Markdown in the training repository. Each time you use it, fill in the issue and attach the current source and test files. Call out the output you want. Here the agent should describe the source path, propose the smallest edit, name the verification, and stop for review. A teammate can copy the template into chat on the approved VS Code setup.
scenes.code:
Read issue [id] and the attached source and tests.
Propose the smallest edit and a regression test.
List the files, validation steps and open questions.
Stop after the plan for human review.
scenes.result: Template: docs/prompts/plan-a-fix.md

scenes.title: Supply current evidence at invocation
scenes.body: Use the template with source files and tests from the same revision.
scenes.narration: Start Plan and paste the filled template. Attach the issue, the source file, and the tests from the revision you intend to change. Check the response against those sources. If the plan talks about a file that does not exist, ask which available evidence supports that claim. These attachments are context for this request. A reusable prompt is easier to trust when the task-specific evidence stays visible.
scenes.code:
Issue #17
order_quantity.py
tests/test_order_quantity.py
scenes.result: Plan names the condition and the missing zero test.

scenes.title: Record a project convention once
scenes.body: Keep the instructions concrete and versioned with the code.
scenes.narration: Open the repository root and confirm the selected Copilot setup. In this example, use the project instructions file in the dot GitHub folder. Add the few conventions we want available when working on this project. Tell the agent where tests go, which test framework is already in use, and where to find the verification command. If the repository already has project instructions, review them before adding overlapping guidance.
scenes.code:
# Order validator conventions
- Use unittest for unit tests under tests/.
- Preserve public signatures unless the issue says otherwise.
- See README.md for the approved verification command.
scenes.result: Saved: .github/copilot-instructions.md

scenes.title: Check that Copilot loaded the instructions
scenes.body: Verify discovery and actual behavior in a new chat.
scenes.narration: Start a fresh session in the same workspace. Use the customizations view to verify that the file is listed. Where references are available, check that the file was included in the request. Then ask for a small plan without repeating the conventions in your prompt. Inspect whether it points to the expected test location and framework. Check discovery and behavior separately so you know what to fix if the result differs.
scenes.code: Plan one regression test for the zero-quantity issue.
scenes.result: File discovered. Plan uses the existing unittest suite.

scenes.title: Give each type of guidance a clear role
scenes.body: Use a task template, project instructions and real review controls.
scenes.narration: The template expresses the current request. The instruction file supplies the project's rules when the selected setup loads it. Permissions and required checks enforce separate boundaries. If your VS Code release offers runnable prompt files, confirm support for the selected harness before using that format. In this lesson the Markdown template works as text you can paste. The next lesson turns a repeated procedure into an invocable skill.
scenes.code:
Prompt template → task request
Instruction file → project conventions
Permissions and checks → enforcement
scenes.result: Review each file where its behavior is observable.

scenes.title: Try a second issue and compare the plan
scenes.body: Change the issue and check which guidance still applies.
scenes.narration: Reuse the template on a second synthetic issue. Replace the issue reference and attachments with the new evidence. Check that the project convention still applies and the plan changes where the new issue calls for it. Review the prompt template and instruction diff with a teammate. You should be able to point to the task inputs, the convention that carried over, and the check that would establish correctness.
scenes.code:
New issue → new attachments → new plan
Same repository → same test conventions
scenes.result: A teammate can reproduce the setup in a fresh chat.

title: What Is a Skill? Build Your First One
subtitle: Agent Skills in VS Code · Intermediate

sources.label: Create Agent Skills in VS Code

scenes.title: Find a task the team repeats
scenes.body: Package a pull request evidence checklist for reuse.
scenes.narration: Suppose your team keeps asking Copilot to organize the same evidence before requesting a review. Each time, the agent needs the issue, a summary of the diff, and the test result. A skill is a package the agent can use when that kind of task comes up. We will start with three steps and one result that a human can inspect before sending it to a teammate.
scenes.code:
Input: issue, diff and test output
Procedure: check and summarize the evidence
Output: a draft for the human author
scenes.result: Chosen skill: prepare pull request evidence.

scenes.title: Name the skill and say when it applies
scenes.body: Use the skill folder supported by the Copilot setup.
scenes.narration: In the training repository, create a project skill named prepare p r evidence. Under the dot GitHub skills folder, give it a directory with the same name and add a file called skill dot M D. The header contains a name and description. State which request it is for, so both the teammate invoking it and the client selecting it have a clear signal.
scenes.code:
---
name: prepare-pr-evidence
description: Draft evidence for a training pull request.
---
scenes.result: .github/skills/prepare-pr-evidence/SKILL.md

scenes.title: Define the steps and intended output
scenes.body: Make missing evidence visible in the draft.
scenes.narration: In the body, ask for the issue, the changed behavior, and the result of a real test run. Define how to handle missing inputs. If the test output is absent, call that out so the author can supply it. Keep this first skill as a short procedure. The human author reviews the resulting draft and decides what to publish. Tool permissions and repository controls still apply.
scenes.code:
1. Read the provided issue and diff.
2. Check the supplied test output.
3. Draft: Issue, Change, Verification, Gaps.
If data is missing, identify the gap.
Return text for the human author to review.
scenes.result: The scope ends with a draft.

scenes.eyebrow: COPILOT · INVOKE IN A FRESH CHAT
scenes.title: Discover and try the skill
scenes.body: Invoke it with the synthetic order validator change.
scenes.narration: Open a fresh Copilot chat in the project. Verify discovery in the customizations view, then invoke the skill through the slash menu when the approved setup supports it. Give it the synthetic issue, the diff, and the passing test output. Read the draft and map each claim back to a supplied source. Check that the procedure gives a teammate a more consistent result than rewriting the request each time.
scenes.code:
/prepare-pr-evidence
Attach issue #17, the diff and the test output.
scenes.result:
Issue #17
Change: zero is rejected.
Verification: four unit tests passed.
Gaps: none in the supplied training evidence.

scenes.title: Check what happens when proof is missing
scenes.body: Run the same skill with the test output omitted.
scenes.narration: Repeat the invocation in a new chat, this time without the test output. Expect the draft to say that verification is missing. If it reports a green run from the issue description alone, tighten the instructions and rerun the case. Now ask an unrelated question, such as explaining a Python expression, and check whether the skill is relevant. This gives you a small repeatable test of behavior and scope.
scenes.code:
Inputs: issue and diff only
Expected: mark verification as missing
scenes.result: Verification gap surfaced for the human author.

scenes.title: Separate procedures from access
scenes.body: A procedure can refer to tools inside the approved boundary.
scenes.narration: Place this skill beside the instruction file from the previous lesson. The instruction file carries project conventions. The skill carries the reusable procedure. Tools perform actions such as reading a file. An approved M C P connection can expose additional tools or resources in another environment. This skill works using supplied files and outputs. Access remains governed by the selected client, its tools, and the organization's settings.
scenes.code:
Instructions → project conventions
Skill → reusable procedure
Tool → callable action
MCP → connection to a server
scenes.result: Review the skill and its dependencies before sharing.

scenes.title: Write a second skill with two test cases
scenes.body: Choose a recurring task and define its limits.
scenes.narration: Pick a second recurring task, such as summarizing a failed training test for the author. Write a name, a description, a short procedure, and the expected output. Try it with complete input and with one item missing. Ask a teammate to judge both responses using the same criteria. Share the versioned file once you can explain when it applies and show that it handles the missing input clearly.
scenes.code:
Candidate: summarize a failing test
Case A: failure output supplied
Case B: failure output missing
scenes.result: An invocable procedure with two observable tests.

title: Build a Workflow with Review Checkpoints
subtitle: Copilot, CI and human review · Intermediate

scenes.title: Map the work before delegating a step
scenes.body: Give every checkpoint an owner and evidence.
scenes.narration: Bring the previous lessons together in one workflow. Start with the issue and plan the smallest verifiable change. Then demonstrate a failing regression, apply the fix, and verify the passing regression. The author reviews the diff and submits the pull request. A teammate reviews it independently. At each checkpoint, write down what evidence lets the work continue and who makes that decision.
scenes.code:
Issue → Plan → Human scope review
Failing test → Fix → Passing tests
Author diff review → PR → Peer review
scenes.result: Each handoff has evidence and an owner.

scenes.title: Review the plan before editing
scenes.body: The author checks the intended behavior and allowed change.
scenes.narration: Use the reusable prompt in Plan with the issue, the validator file, and its tests. The agent proposes an edit and verification steps. Review the suggestion against the issue yourself. In this example, it may add a regression test and change one comparison. If it proposes a new dependency or changes the public interface, revise the plan with the original requirement visible before moving into Agent.
scenes.code:
Keep is_valid_quantity(quantity: int) -> bool.
Add an assertion for quantity zero.
Change only the boundary comparison.
scenes.result: Author accepts scope after checking the issue.

scenes.title: Verify that the test detects the defect
scenes.body: Let the expected failure authorize the next coding step.
scenes.narration: Add the new test first and run it using the approved runner. A useful failure identifies the zero case and shows that the validator returned true. If the failure comes from a broken import, fix the test setup and repeat the run before accepting the evidence. The checkpoint requires a failing assertion tied to the issue. Record the result and use it to justify applying the small fix.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
Expected before the fix
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false

scenes.title: Stop when validation remains red
scenes.body: Review the approved change and require the expected passing run.
scenes.narration: Ask Agent to make the agreed edit. Check the diff and rerun the same suite. If another test starts failing or the expected regression still fails, return to the fix and inspect the new behavior. In a passing run, capture the command and the result. This pause keeps a plausible explanation from becoming your only evidence. It also helps keep the next review focused on the actual change.
scenes.code:
Pass → attach the test output
Fail → inspect, adjust and rerun
scenes.result: All four tests pass in the completed example.

scenes.title: Prepare evidence for the pull request
scenes.body: Tie the issue, patch and checks to the same change.
scenes.narration: Use the skill from the previous lesson to draft the handoff. Provide the linked training issue, the diff, and the output you just checked. Review its draft and correct any claim that does not match those artifacts. Push the feature branch and open the pull request through your approved workflow. The configured checks run on the reviewed change. A passing local or runner result gives the reviewer additional evidence.
scenes.code:
Closes #17
Changed: reject zero at the validator boundary
Regression: test_rejects_zero
Verification: four unit tests passed
scenes.result: PR #42 is ready for separate peer review.

scenes.title: Let the peer make the review decision
scenes.body: A teammate reviews the revision and required checks with GitHub CLI.
scenes.narration: The peer now uses the approved terminal and their own account. They view the pull request, read the diff and check the required results. If the evidence is sufficient, they can submit an approval. If something is missing, they can request changes and name what needs to be checked. The repository's configured checks and review rules protect the merge. The agent's draft helps prepare the handoff.
scenes.code:
gh pr view 42
gh pr diff 42
gh pr checks 42 --required
scenes.result: Peer decision: approve or request a specific change.

scenes.title: Dry-run both outcomes
scenes.body: Demonstrate a successful handoff and one blocked branch.
scenes.narration: Try the workflow with a teammate on the synthetic repository. During the first run, walk all the way to the peer decision with passing checks and a small patch. During the second, introduce missing test evidence or a failing required check and say where you stop. Write down the evidence needed to resume and who decides. That is the workflow you can reuse on the next issue.
scenes.code:
A: Scope accepted, tests pass, peer reviews
B: Verification missing, work returns to author
scenes.result: A documented workflow with a tested stop condition.
